What Is the AI Data Risk Checker?

The AI Data Risk Checker is a simple self-assessment tool designed to help UK business owners understand what risks they might be taking — knowingly or not — when they use AI tools with their company data.

It asks a short series of questions about how your business currently uses AI, what data you're putting into those systems, and what controls you have in place. At the end, it gives you a plain-language summary of where your exposure sits and what, if anything, you should be thinking about.

It won't give you a legal opinion. It won't audit your systems. What it will do is help you have a more informed conversation — with your IT team, your legal advisers, or with us.

Why This Matters More Than Most People Realise

Most businesses using AI tools haven't thought carefully about where their data goes. That's not a criticism — the tools are easy to use, the interfaces are friendly, and nobody hands you a data flow diagram when you sign up for a free trial.

But when you paste a client contract into ChatGPT, upload a financial report to an AI summariser, or use a browser extension that reads your emails, data is moving somewhere. Sometimes it's used to train models. Sometimes it's stored in ways you haven't agreed to. Sometimes it crosses jurisdictions in ways that matter for compliance.

None of this means AI tools are dangerous or that you should stop using them. It means it's worth knowing what you're actually doing.

The question isn't whether AI is safe. It's whether you know what you've agreed to, and whether that matches what your clients and regulators expect of you.

How to Use the Checker

Work through the questions honestly. The tool is only useful if you answer based on what actually happens in your business, not what you think should happen or what your policy documents say.

If you're not sure of an answer — for example, you don't know whether a tool your team uses stores data on EU servers — mark it as unknown. Uncertainty is itself useful information. It tells you where to look.

The whole thing takes around five minutes. You don't need a technical background to complete it.

Understanding Your Results

Low Risk

Your current AI usage appears to involve limited data exposure. You're either using AI with non-sensitive information, you have clear controls in place, or both. This doesn't mean you can stop paying attention — AI tools change their terms regularly — but you're in a reasonable position.

Moderate Risk

There are one or more areas where your data handling deserves a closer look. This might mean a tool you're using has unclear data retention policies, you're processing client or financial data through consumer AI products, or your team is using AI tools without a consistent policy. None of these are emergencies, but they're worth addressing before they become problems.

Higher Risk

Your current setup has meaningful gaps between what you're doing and what you'd want to be doing if a client asked you directly. This is more common than people expect — particularly in professional services, finance, and healthcare adjacent businesses. The good news is that most of these issues are solvable, often without replacing the tools you already use.

Common Risk Areas the Checker Covers

  • Consumer AI tools used for business data — Tools built for personal use often have terms that permit broad data use. Using them with client data, financial records, or commercially sensitive information carries risks that business-grade alternatives don't.
  • Data residency and jurisdiction — Where your data is processed and stored matters, particularly for businesses subject to UK GDPR or sector-specific regulation. Many popular AI tools process data outside the UK and EU by default.
  • Model training on your inputs — Some AI services use your inputs to improve their models unless you explicitly opt out. This is worth understanding before you share anything proprietary.
  • No internal AI policy — If your team is using AI tools without guidance on what's acceptable, you don't have visibility into your own risk profile. That's a gap worth closing.
  • Third-party integrations — AI features built into tools you already use (email clients, CRMs, document editors) often have separate data terms from the main product. These are easy to miss.

What You Can Do About It

Depending on your results, the options range from simple to more involved.

For lower-risk adjustments

  • Review the data terms for the AI tools your team uses most often
  • Write a short internal policy — even a one-page document — covering what data can and can't go into AI tools
  • Switch to business-tier versions of tools you already use, which typically offer stronger data protections

For more significant gaps

If your results suggest meaningful exposure — particularly if you handle client data, financial records, or anything regulated — it's worth looking at whether a private deployment makes sense for your situation.

Private AI deployments run models inside your own infrastructure, or locally on your own hardware. Data never leaves your environment. There's no third-party retention, no jurisdiction question, and no dependency on a vendor's terms of service. For some businesses, this is the right answer. For others, a well-configured business-tier cloud tool is sufficient.

The honest answer is: it depends on what you're doing with AI and what your obligations are. We can help you work that out.

A Note on What This Tool Isn't

The AI Data Risk Checker is a starting point, not a compliance certification. It doesn't replace a data protection audit, legal advice, or a conversation with your DPO if you have one.

What it does is give you a structured way to think about something most businesses haven't thought about systematically. That's useful in itself — and it gives you a foundation for any more formal assessment you might want to do afterwards.

If You Want to Go Further

If your results raise questions you'd like to explore — whether that's understanding private AI deployment options, building an internal AI policy, or working out which tools are actually appropriate for your use case — we're happy to have that conversation.

We work with UK businesses on practical AI implementation. That includes helping companies use AI safely, not just effectively. The two aren't in conflict; they just both require some thought.
